analysis.one_liner: Cuts the federal estate and gift tax rate from 40% to a flat 20%.
analysis.headline: The bill got 3 cosponsors and has not moved since it was referred to two House committees in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cut the top federal tax on large estates and large lifetime gifts from 40% to a flat 20%, for deaths and gifts after December 31, 2024. Only the biggest estates pay the estate tax, so the cut would go almost entirely to heirs of the wealthiest families. It would also cut the gift tax, letting wealthy people hand money to relatives during their lifetime at half the current rate.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs and families holding the largest estates — the estate tax only applies above a multi-million-dollar exemption, so virtually all of the benefit goes to the top few tenths of a percent of households. Wealthy people planning large lifetime gifts also gain, because the gift tax rate would drop in step with the estate tax [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the estate tax rate schedule with a flat 20% rate, cutting the top rate from 40% to 20% on taxable estates [S2].
Applies the same 20% rate to gifts and generation-skipping transfers, so wealth can be passed between generations during life or at death at half the current top rate [S2].
Exempts the bill's revenue loss from the statutory PAYGO scorecards, so the cost does not trigger automatic spending offsets [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Every dollar the estate tax collects is a dollar not collected elsewhere, so the cost lands on taxpayers generally through larger deficits or reduced government services. Non-wealthy households get no direct benefit from the rate cut because their estates are far below the taxable threshold.

drawbacks.text: Cutting the top rate from 40% to 20% would cut federal revenue roughly in half on the largest estates, worsening deficits or forcing offsetting cuts [S2].
Because the bill also lowers the gift tax rate, it makes it cheaper to move large wealth between generations during life, not just at death [S2].
The bill's text excludes its own budget cost from PAYGO enforcement scorecards, removing the automatic guardrail that would otherwise require the revenue loss to be paid for [S2].

Supporters' usual argument — protecting family farms and small businesses from forced sales — is only partly addressed here: the bill cuts the rate but does not raise the exemption, so the estates it helps are overwhelmingly the very largest ones [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concentrated: heirs of multi-million-dollar estates would pay 20 cents on the taxable dollar instead of 40. The cost is diffuse: a smaller federal treasury, spread across everyone else through deficits or reduced spending. There is no provision in the bill directed at middle- or working-income families.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Budget committees in January 2025 and has taken no further step — no committee vote, no floor action — while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Jodey Arrington introduced the bill on January 22, 2025, with Rep. Bishop as an original cosponsor [S1][S2][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Budget Committee [S4].
It attracted 3 cosponsors total — 2 of 223 House Republicans and 1 of 217 House Democrats — and has had no action since referral [S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained: the estate tax is unchanged and the bill is simply sitting in committee. Taxpayers benefit relative to passage because the revenue has not been cut, but the status quo simply continues.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo holds; no one has gained yet

for.name: Rep. Jodey Arrington
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer tax rate to 20%

for.name: Rep. Bishop
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as an original cosponsor at introduction

sides.party_line_note: Support was minimal and overwhelmingly Republican: 2 of 223 House Republicans and 1 of 217 House Democrats cosponsored, with no Democratic push behind the bill [S3].

industries.industry: Heirs of the largest estates (top fraction of 1% of households)
industries.note: A 20% flat rate on estates and gifts would roughly halve the tax owed on the largest transfers of family wealth. The revenue foregone is carried by taxpayers at large, and no other household qualifies for the benefit [S2].

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth advisory services
industries.note: Lower rates change the calculus for trusts, gifts, and generation-skipping arrangements, shifting demand within the estate-planning industry. The effect on practitioners is secondary to the direct benefit to wealthy families.

analysis.trajectory: With only 3 cosponsors and no committee action more than a year into the session, this standalone bill is very unlikely to get a vote. Estate-tax changes of this kind, if enacted at all, would more likely ride inside a larger tax package negotiated by party leadership.
